To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the scopolamine test is an effective tool for identifying individuals at risk for Alzheimer’s disease, as well as for monitoring cognitive change and Aβ-related cognitive decline over time.
disruption of cholinergic transmission, within a cognitive stress test paradigm, is a reliable predictor of Aβ-related changes in cognition and brain amyloid load, after a 3-year delay interval.
cognitive performance on the scopolamine cognitive stress test is related to both amyloid PET imaging results and cognitive change, in preclinical Alzheimer disease after a 2.25-year interval.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the early diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease.

the development of a novel, non-invasive cognitive challenge paradigm, the scopolamine test, to identify individuals who have an elevated risk for AD and are likely to develop cognitive impairment within 2 years.

the development of a novel, non-pharmacological cognitive stress test, the scopolamine cognitive stress test (SCT), to screen older adults for early signs of cognitive impairment and risk for Alzheimer’s disease.

the SCT is an effective and sensitive screening tool for the identification of individuals at risk of developing AD.
the SCT, in conjunction with PET imaging, is a useful tool for identifying preclinical AD and for monitoring disease progression.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cholinergic disruption, as measured by the SCT, is indicative of cognitive decline in the preclinical stage of AD, and is related to the presence of amyloid pathology.

the SCT, as a cognitive stress test, is a promising tool to identify individuals in the earliest stages of AD, and that it is a promising tool for monitoring the progression of cognitive decline in preclinical AD.

a cholinergic challenge test may be a useful tool to identify preclinical individuals at risk for developing AD.
